USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the existing Section 301 stack ($50B at 25% plus List 3 at 10%) and use the already-scheduled January 1, 2019 step-up of List 3 to 25% as leverage, rather than adding a new tariff tranche now. Engage China through the planned Trump–Xi meeting at the November G-20 without new U.S. commitments: talks should test whether Beijing will put enforceable IP, tech-transfer, and non-tariff barrier offers on the table. Do not trade the current posture for another purchase-only package of the May type, and do not roll back tariffs until structural terms are real.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modest, not high or existential. U.S. macro is still resilient—Michigan sentiment 98.6, industrial production up about 1.5% over the window, CPI only a modest 0.8% rise—so this is not a +0.5 GDP-drag reading. The threat is real on three narrower fronts. First, a key export sector is already hit: China matched Lists 1–2 and then put 5–10% tariffs on ~$60B of U.S. goods (2018-09-24), after earlier targeting soybeans, autos, and aircraft; USDA had to authorize up to $12B in farm relief, with ~$3.6B earmarked for soybeans after prices fell about $2/bushel. Second, the tariff campaign is not yet delivering the intended bilateral adjustment: U.S. goods imports from China rose from $43.9B (May) to $52.1B (October) as importers front-ran List 3, while U.S. exports to China fell 11.6% and the goods deficit widened from −$66.6B to −$76.5B. Third, CNY depreciation of ~9.7% (6.32 to 6.93) is offsetting a large share of the 10% List 3 bite, and the mid-October equity selloff (VIX to ~25 on Oct 10–11) plus IMF warnings show financial markets are starting to price a longer fight. Those costs sit against unused U.S. leverage—China has less remaining U.S. goods to tariff, Chinese equities were already down ~20% by September, and reserves slipped ~$56B—so the net reading is a mild threat (+0.20), not an opportunity to press harder immediately.

Action should be negotiate, not escalate or concede. List 3 only took effect September 24; another hike now would land on more consumer goods, raise midterm and farm-belt costs, and risk a non-tariff Chinese response just as a G-20 leader meeting has been agreed (first direct leader talks since August). August working-level talks produced no structural movement, and the May 19 joint statement (China to “significantly increase” purchases; Mnuchin “on hold”) collapsed within ten days because purchase promises did not address the March 22 Section 301 findings. Keep the January 1 25% clock running as the bargaining chip; reopen talks aimed at IP/tech-transfer remedies; treat any Chinese purchase offer as a side payment, not a settlement.
key_factors: Section 301 coverage now ~$250B after List 3 (10%) took effect 2018-09-24, with a scheduled rise to 25% on 2019-01-01 already on the table
China has retaliated through the $50B match plus 5–10% tariffs on ~$60B of U.S. goods, concentrating pain on soybeans and other farm exports
U.S. real economy still firm (sentiment, IP) but bilateral trade is moving the wrong way: China imports front-ran tariffs while U.S. exports to China fell ~12% and the goods deficit widened
CNY depreciation of ~10% is blunting U.S. tariff leverage
Trump–Xi G-20 meeting is scheduled; August talks went nowhere and the May purchase-only truce collapsed
October market selloff and Fed tightening raise the second-order cost of an immediate further tariff tranche

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR Section 301 report finds China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable; Trump directs tariffs, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
US and China joint statement: China agrees to significantly increase purchases; Mnuchin says trade war is on hold.
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions including 25% tariffs on ~$50B. Truce collapses.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% on ~$200B effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes 5–10% tariffs on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B.
U.S. exports to mainland China fell from $10.40B (May) to $9.19B (October), −11.6% over the window.
U.S. imports from China rose from $43.87B (May) to $52.08B (October), +18.7%, consistent with front-running of List 3.
U.S. goods trade deficit widened from −$66.6B (May) to −$76.5B (October).
CNY depreciated from 6.32 to 6.93 per USD (~9.7%), offsetting a large share of the new 10% List 3 tariff.
Michigan consumer sentiment still high at 98.6 in October; U.S. domestic demand not showing a trade-war collapse.
VIX spiked to 22.96–24.98 on Oct 10–11 before easing to 17.4 on Oct 17.
Trump and Xi agreed to meet at the November G-20 in Buenos Aires, the first direct leader talks since August.
USDA authorized up to $12B in farm relief; initial MFP soybean rate $1.65/bu, ~$3.63B of the first $4.7B tranche.
As of Oct 17 the U.S. had three rounds of 301 tariffs on $250B of Chinese goods plus steel/aluminum, and was pairing that with bilateral deals to pressure Beijing.
Mid-October equity selloff attributed in part to Fed hikes plus the US–China trade war; IMF had warned the $200B tariffs could harm growth.
